summary: "Bistable images such as the duck–rabbit support multiple mutually incompatible interpretations, typically reported one at a time in humans. The paper asks whether multimodal LLMs (LLaVA family) show similar report behavior and what internal computations support it, along two dimensions: *modulability* (can reports be biased by bottom-up visual cues and top-down linguistic priors?) and *exclusivity* (do responses commit to a single interpretation?), tested on the canonical duck–rabbit and on synthetic Visual Anagrams to mitigate memorization confounds. Behaviorally, visual and linguistic manipulations shift reports in human-consistent ways and responses remain predominantly exclusive; mechanistically, these effects arise from competing image-token representations, distinct pathways for bottom-up and top-down modulation, and a link between exclusive reporting and object-count encoding."
